summary:
Burdur Province sits under Türkiye's national legal and policing framework, which leaves no room for a separate provincial regime. The Turkish Criminal Code remains in force as written; the leaked 11th Judicial Package reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025 would add explicit prohibition of conduct deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality', with penalties of up to three years in prison, and up to four years for taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony. The draft had not been adopted when reported, and its pending status has not stopped authorities from behaving as though the prohibitions already operate.

That gap between draft text and enforcement practice is the central operational risk for a trans visitor. In 2025, police in Beyoğlu, Istanbul stopped roughly twenty trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for 'General Information Gathering' (GBT) background checks before release. Rights lawyers cited in the reporting argue these checks breach Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One woman detained in those operations reported that officers imposed no fines but documented her anyway, and noted that the new law had not yet been passed even as it was being enforced against her.

Checkpoint interactions carry a direct outing exposure for anyone whose presentation does not match their passport. Foreign nationals in Türkiye are required to produce original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. Every stop is an occasion on which documents are compared against appearance.

Violence against trans people in Türkiye is lethal and the state response is asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim herself was referred for arrest, a sequence activists treat as evidence of state policy rather than isolated error.

Transition-related care is being restricted through administrative regulation rather than legislation. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added 'gender reassignment' as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the 'other' option and required electronic reports to be issued. The effect is to place trans patients in a named, trackable category in official records and to narrow access to transition care.

The draft package would push that restriction further. It would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care including surgery from 18 to 25 and impose a mandatory permanent-infertility condition, penalising health professionals who provide such care and exposing patients to prison terms of their own. Fifteen Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association have publicly opposed the draft.

Pride organising remains a flashpoint. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through the 2025 event, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia and entrenching discrimination against LGBT people and those who support them.

Prison exposure, should a trans visitor be detained, is governed by segregation and placement on registered sex. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Coordination by Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation; accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025, confirmed that Türkiye places trans prisoners according to registered sex, a trans man having been held in a women's prison.

Prison Insider's country profile on Türkiye, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and drawing on ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches of LGBT detainees, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration runs on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

The depth of the regime is measurable. Human Rights Watch's October 2025 assessment described the draft package as one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades, and Kaos GL's 2025 report 'A major siege against LGBTI+ people in 2025: Hostility turned into state policy', launched by lawyer Kerem Dikmen, finds that hostility became institutionalised through senior officials' hate speech and instructions issued to public institutions under a 'Year of the Family' banner, creating a climate that encouraged human-rights violations, with regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricting freedom of expression and artistic freedom.

For a trans visitor, the practical consequence is that the legal status of conduct is unstable, that enforcement operates ahead of legislation, and that document checks, detention and any contact with the prison or health systems each carry an outing and detention exposure.
tangentialFactors:
Compared with most European destinations, Türkiye's distinguishing feature is not residual prejudice but the direction of travel. Human Rights Watch characterised the leaked draft as the most significant step back on LGBT rights in decades, while Kaos GL recorded 313 violations in 2025, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, including 299 detention decisions, 256 of them through formal channels and 43 taken off the record.

The 2025 pattern is documented across both state action and state rhetoric. Kaos GL's report findings, presented by lawyer Kerem Dikmen at the launch, describe a 'Year of the Family' policy banner under which instructions were issued to public institutions and supervisory bodies applied pressure on freedom of expression and artistic freedom. Human Rights Write and Human Rights Watch reporting identifies protection of 'the family' and 'public morals' as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma of LGBT people.

Historical evidence supports the depth of the pattern rather than its novelty. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, based on more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. It predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as background, not as a statement of current law.

Burdur Province has no enforcement or incident data in the current source inventory. The province appears in the record only as an administrative unit inside the national framework, and the documented instances of police checks, pride restrictions, care regulation and prison deaths cited above occurred in other provinces and should be read as indicators of national practice rather than as findings about Burdur.

outOfScopeNotes:
No enforcement or incident data specific to Burdur Province appears in the source inventory. Whether police in Burdur conduct GBT-style stops, how local hospitals apply the September 2025 Health Ministry regulation, and whether the province operates any LGBT-targeted checkpoint activity remain unresolved and are not sourced here.

The current status of the 11th Judicial Package as of the writing of this record is unresolved. The sources describe it as a leaked draft before the government in October 2025, opposed by 15 Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association; whether it has since been adopted or amended is not established by the inventory.

The parent framework records 313 violations and 299 detention decisions in 2025 in the Kaos GL count, while the current summary references a Kaos GL report published February 2026 with different figures for right-to-life violations and torture or ill-treatment. The two Kaos GL datasets cover different publications and the relationship between them is not resolved by the available material.

The Kaos GL 2025 report's specific count of 299 detention decisions is taken from the parent framework record and is attributed there to Kaos GL's 2025 reporting; the report launch material cited in the current inventory supports the finding of institutionalised state policy but does not restate those figures.

The September 2025 Health Ministry regulation is described in the inventory through secondary reporting. The regulation's text, its precise scope for provincial health directorates, and any transitional arrangements for patients already in treatment are not established here.

Whether Türkiye's national anti-discrimination or hate-crime provisions can be invoked in practice by trans visitors, and how consistently prosecutors treat anti-trans violence as hate-motivated, is only partly evidenced: the inventory records six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025 with three classified as hate killings by rights organisations, and the Bakırköy 2024 case in which the victim was referred for arrest while the attacker was released. Consistency of prosecution outcomes across provinces is unresolved.
